transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, the main thing that pushed me to come in is… I guess I’m having trouble really taking in what people are saying sometimes. Like my wife will be talking to me about something practical, usually about my cousin’s appointments or who’s giving him a ride, and I’m looking right at her — I mean I’m not walking away or ignoring her — but then a minute later I realize I only caught part of it. Sometimes not even half of it, honestly.

It’s embarrassing because she’ll say, “I just told you that,” and she’s right. I was sitting there, I heard her voice, I knew she was talking, but it’s like it didn’t fully land. That’s been bothering me enough that I thought I should come talk to someone about it.
Have you ever had the experience of hearing things that others don’t seem to hear, or feeling like voices or sounds are interfering with your ability to focus on what someone is saying?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’m trying to think carefully because I don’t want to answer too fast and miss what you’re getting at, but I haven’t had anything like voices that other people can’t hear, or sounds that feel like they’re coming from nowhere.

It’s more like… if someone is talking to me, especially if there’s other normal noise around, I may lose the thread. But I wouldn’t say there are voices interfering or anything like that. Nothing that seems unusual in that way, at least not that I’ve noticed.
Have you noticed any changes in the way things look, feel, or sound—like seeing things that aren’t there, or hearing sounds that don’t seem real to you?

No, not that I’ve noticed. I mean, I’ve never had a situation where I’m seeing something that isn’t there, or hearing something and thinking, “Where did that come from?” when nobody else hears it.

Sometimes ordinary sounds can pull my attention around — like if there’s a TV on or people talking nearby — but that’s just regular noise, not anything strange or unreal. As far as things looking different or feeling unreal, I don’t think so. I haven’t had that kind of experience.
Have you ever had strong beliefs or ideas that other people around you don’t seem to share, even after they’ve tried to convince you otherwise?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I have opinions like anybody else, and sometimes I can be stubborn about practical things at home, like how something should be handled, but not in the sense that people are trying to convince me I’m wrong about something and I just can’t let go of it.

I’m trying to think if there’s anything like that, because I know sometimes people can have beliefs they don’t realize are unusual. But I can’t think of anything where my wife or family is saying, “That’s not real,” or “Nobody else thinks that,” and I’m still completely convinced. Nothing like that comes to mind.
Have you been feeling down, depressed, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even if just for a few days a week or part of the day?

I’m not really sure I’d describe it that way. I mean, I have normal ups and downs, I guess — like anybody, I can get frustrated or kind of worn out by things — but I haven’t noticed a stretch where I’d say I’m depressed, or where I’m not interested in the things I usually like.

I’m trying to think about the “few days a week or part of the day” part, because maybe there are moments where I’m just not in the mood for much, but that feels more like ordinary mood stuff to me, not like a clear change. So… no, I don’t think I’ve been feeling down or losing interest in that way.

Have you had times when your mood was unusually high, or you felt more energetic or restless than usual, where you were doing things more quickly or taking on more than usual, even if only for a few days?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve had days where I feel a little more motivated, like I finally decide to get a bunch of small things done around the house, but I wouldn’t call it unusually high or anything like that.

I’m trying to picture what you mean — like being energized in a way that’s out of character, or taking on a lot more than I normally would — and I can’t really think of times like that. I don’t have stretches where I’m suddenly moving faster, talking faster, or feeling like I’m on some kind of roll for days. If anything, it’s more like normal variation from day to day. Some days I get more done, some days I don’t, but nothing that has stood out to me as unusual.
Have you had trouble feeling pleasure or interest in things that usually give you enjoyment, even for a few days at a time?

I don’t think so, no. I mean, I have days where I’m not really in the mood to do much, or I’ll sort of drift around and not start something I’d usually enjoy, but once I actually do it, I still enjoy it. It doesn’t feel like the enjoyment is gone.

Like if I watch something I like, or spend time on a hobby, or talk with family, I can still get pleasure out of it. Sometimes I’m just slow to get going, or I’ll put things off and then realize later I would’ve liked doing them. But that seems different from not feeling interest or pleasure for days at a time.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed that. Nothing where I’d say things I normally enjoy have stopped feeling enjoyable.
Over the past two weeks, have you had days where you felt down or had little interest or pleasure in doing things for most of the day, more days than not?

No, not more days than not. I’m trying to think back over the last two weeks specifically, because sometimes it’s easy to blur days together, but I don’t remember having most of the day where I felt down or like I couldn’t enjoy anything.

There might be parts of a day where I feel kind of blah or unmotivated, but it doesn’t really last the whole day, and it doesn’t feel like a loss of interest or pleasure exactly. If something enjoyable comes up, I can still enjoy it. So I’d say no, I haven’t had that happening most days.

Have you noticed any problems with staying focused or keeping your attention on tasks, like reading a few sentences and realizing you haven’t taken in what you just read, or having trouble following through on something you started?

Yes, that does happen. It’s not every single thing I do, but with things that take steady concentration, I notice it.

Like if I sit down to work out a catering order, I’ll start off thinking, okay, I’m going to go through the list, check the quantities, make sure I’m not missing anything — and at first I’m fine. But then after a little while I’ll realize I’ve been looking at the same section and I don’t actually know what I just read. It’s like my eyes kept moving but my mind went somewhere else. Then I have to go back over the same notes again, sometimes more than once, which is frustrating because it feels like it should be simple.

The same kind of thing happens on parish planning calls. I’ll be listening at the start, and I really do intend to follow along, but if it goes on for a while, my attention kind of drifts. Then someone refers back to something that was just said, and I’m trying to piece it together from the notes or from context because I missed part of it. I’m not trying to ignore anyone — I just sort of lose the thread.

So yes, staying focused through a task or following through without having to re-check myself can be a problem.
Do you often find that you need to put in extra effort to maintain focus, or that your mind wanders frequently, even when you’re trying to pay attention to something important?

Yes, I do. I mean, I can make myself pay attention for a bit, especially if I know it matters, but it feels like I’m having to keep pulling myself back over and over.

With something like a catering order, I’ll sit down and think, “Okay, just go through this carefully,” and I’ll start fine. But then before very long I realize my mind has wandered, and I’m looking at the notes but I haven’t really taken them in. Then I have to go back over the same part again like I never read it in the first place.

It’s similar on parish planning calls. I’ll be listening, and I’m intending to follow everything, but after a while I lose the thread. Then I’m trying to catch up from context or check my notes, and sometimes the notes aren’t even very helpful because I wasn’t fully focused when I wrote them.

So yes, it’s not that I don’t care or I’m not trying. I’m trying, but it takes extra effort to stay with it, and my mind still wanders.
Have you had trouble feeling pleasure or enjoyment in things you usually like, even for a few days at a time?

I don’t think so, no. I mean, I have days where I’m a little flat or I don’t feel like starting something, but once I’m actually doing something I usually like, I can still enjoy it.

I wouldn’t say I’ve had a stretch of a few days where things just didn’t feel pleasurable. It’s more like sometimes I’m slow to get going, or I’m distracted, but if I’m around something pleasant or something I normally enjoy, I still get something out of it. So I don’t think I’ve had that problem in the way you’re asking.
Have you noticed any other changes in your thinking, like trouble remembering things, making decisions, or organizing your thoughts, even if it’s been subtle?

Yes, I have noticed it, mostly with remembering things I meant to do. It’s not like I’m forgetting who people are or anything dramatic like that, but these little practical things slip by me, and then I realize later and feel annoyed with myself.

For example, I meant to return a call from the doctor’s office recently, and I had it in my head like, “I need to call them back,” but then the day moved on and I just didn’t do it. And picking up a prescription — same kind of thing. I’ll know it needs to be done, and it’s not that I don’t think it’s important, but it just sort of falls out of the front of my mind until later.

Leaving the house on time has been an issue too, especially for one of my cousin’s appointments. I’ll think I have enough time, and then I get caught up or lose track of what I still need to do before leaving, and suddenly I’m rushing. It’s subtle in the sense that each thing by itself doesn’t seem huge, but when it keeps happening, it starts to feel like I’m not managing things as smoothly as I used to.

Have you ever felt like you were detached from yourself, like you were observing your own thoughts or actions from outside your body, or like the world around you wasn’t quite real, even if just for brief moments?

No, I don’t think so. At least not in the way you’re describing it.

I’ve had moments where I’m distracted or kind of mentally elsewhere, like I realize I wasn’t really taking in what was happening, but I don’t feel like I’m outside my body watching myself or anything like that. And the world doesn’t seem unreal to me. It’s more ordinary than that — like my attention drifts, not like I’m detached from myself.

So, no, I haven’t really noticed anything like that.
Have you ever had moments where you felt like your thoughts were not your own, or that someone else could hear or influence them?

No, I can’t say I’ve ever had that. I mean, I’ve had plenty of times where my thoughts feel scattered or I’m not following my own train of thought very well, but they still feel like mine.

I’ve never felt like someone else put a thought in my head, or like my thoughts were being broadcast or heard by other people. And I don’t feel like anyone can control or influence them in that way. If I’m influenced by someone, it’s more the normal kind of thing, like somebody says something and then I think about it, not like they’re reaching into my mind or anything.

So no, I haven’t noticed anything like that.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your memory or thinking that have gotten worse over time, like forgetting important events or struggling with tasks that used to be easy for you?

I wouldn’t say it’s been some big, dramatic decline, like I’m forgetting major life events or suddenly can’t do things I used to know how to do. It’s more these everyday things that I meant to take care of, and then they just don’t happen unless something reminds me.

Like I mentioned, returning a call from the doctor’s office — I knew I needed to do it, and I even had that thought more than once, but somehow the day went by and I still hadn’t done it. Same with picking up a prescription. It wasn’t that I didn’t care or didn’t understand it was important; it just slipped out of my mind at the wrong time.

And leaving the house on time has been another one. There was one of my cousin’s appointments where I needed to be ready and out the door, and I thought I was managing the time okay, but then I realized I was behind and rushing. So it’s more that kind of forgetfulness or losing track of what I’m supposed to be doing next. It’s frustrating, but I don’t think of it as me forgetting big important events so much as missing these practical day-to-day things.

Can you describe how long you’ve been experiencing these difficulties with attention, focus, and forgetfulness, and whether you feel they are significantly affecting your ability to function in your daily life?

It’s been, I’d say, noticeably harder for about 11 months now. I can kind of place it because it lines up with when my cousin moved in with us after surgery. Before that, I’m not saying I was perfectly organized or anything, but it didn’t feel like it was getting in the way in the same way.

Since then, with more going on at home and more things to keep track of, I’ve noticed the attention and forgetfulness more. It’s not like I can’t function at all, but it does affect my day-to-day life. I’ll miss little but important things, or I’ll need more reminders, or I’ll lose track of time and then everything becomes rushed. So yes, it’s affecting me, just maybe not in a catastrophic way — more like a constant, frustrating interference.
Have you had similar difficulties with attention, focus, and forgetfulness going back to your childhood or adolescence, or do you feel these problems started more recently, in adulthood?

I think some of it does go way back, actually. It’s not like I would have described it the same way when I was a kid, of course, but looking back, there were signs.

Even in grade school, before I was 12, I remember teachers telling my parents things like, “He’s bright, but he’s always daydreaming,” or that I wasn’t finishing my work unless someone kept reminding me. I’d leave homework in my desk instead of bringing it home, or I’d do part of something and then sort of drift off and not complete the classwork. It wasn’t that I didn’t understand it — that was the frustrating part, I think, for teachers and probably my parents too. It was more like I just wasn’t staying with it.

So, the problems feel more noticeable recently as an adult, especially with more responsibilities, but when you ask whether there were similar patterns in childhood, yes, I think there were. They just weren’t framed the same way back then.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. I mean, I can make myself pay attention for a bit, especially if I know it matters, but it feels like I’m having to keep pulling myself back over and over.

With something like a catering order, I’ll sit down and think, “Okay, just go through this carefully,” and I’ll start fine. But then before very long I realize my mind has wandered, and I’m looking at the notes but I haven’t really taken them in. Then I have to go back over the same part again like I never read it in the first place.

It’s similar on parish planning calls. I’ll be listening, and I’m intending to follow everything, but after a while I lose the thread. Then I’m trying to catch up from context or check my notes, and sometimes the notes aren’t even very helpful because I wasn’t fully focused when I wrote them.

So yes, it’s not that I don’t care or I’m not trying. I’m trying, but it takes extra effort to stay with it, and my mind still wanders.

doctor.intent: Assess the presence of a key depressive symptom (anhedonia) to rule out major depressive disorder (F32.9 or F33.9) versus non-affective disorders like ADHD or other cognitive issues (F06.8).
doctor.question: Have you had trouble feeling pleasure or enjoyment in things you usually like, even for a few days at a time?

target_item.reason: The question asks about reduced pleasure or enjoyment (anhedonia), which is a mood/depression symptom not covered by the provided ADHD inattentive symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, no. I mean, I have days where I’m a little flat or I don’t feel like starting something, but once I’m actually doing something I usually like, I can still enjoy it.

I wouldn’t say I’ve had a stretch of a few days where things just didn’t feel pleasurable. It’s more like sometimes I’m slow to get going, or I’m distracted, but if I’m around something pleasant or something I normally enjoy, I still get something out of it. So I don’t think I’ve had that problem in the way you’re asking.

doctor.intent: Assessing for presence of a neurocognitive disorder, particularly in attention and concentration domains, which could point toward F06.8 if cognitive deficits are primary and not better explained by another condition.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any other changes in your thinking, like trouble remembering things, making decisions, or organizing your thoughts, even if it’s been subtle?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: Lately I’ve forgotten things I meant to do, like returning a call from the doctor’s office, picking up a prescription, or leaving the house on time for one of my cousin’s appointments.
target_item.reason: The question is most directly asking about trouble remembering things in daily life, which matches forgetting calls, prescriptions, and appointments.

patient.answer:
Yes, I have noticed it, mostly with remembering things I meant to do. It’s not like I’m forgetting who people are or anything dramatic like that, but these little practical things slip by me, and then I realize later and feel annoyed with myself.

For example, I meant to return a call from the doctor’s office recently, and I had it in my head like, “I need to call them back,” but then the day moved on and I just didn’t do it. And picking up a prescription — same kind of thing. I’ll know it needs to be done, and it’s not that I don’t think it’s important, but it just sort of falls out of the front of my mind until later.

Leaving the house on time has been an issue too, especially for one of my cousin’s appointments. I’ll think I have enough time, and then I get caught up or lose track of what I still need to do before leaving, and suddenly I’m rushing. It’s subtle in the sense that each thing by itself doesn’t seem huge, but when it keeps happening, it starts to feel like I’m not managing things as smoothly as I used to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms that meet the criteria for a dissociative disorder (F06.8), particularly by assessing if there are episodes of depersonalization, derealization, or other non-reality-based disruptions in cognition or perception.
doctor.question: Have you ever felt like you were detached from yourself, like you were observing your own thoughts or actions from outside your body, or like the world around you wasn’t quite real, even if just for brief moments?

target_item.reason: The question is about depersonalization or derealization experiences, which are not covered by the provided ADHD inattentive symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so. At least not in the way you’re describing it.

I’ve had moments where I’m distracted or kind of mentally elsewhere, like I realize I wasn’t really taking in what was happening, but I don’t feel like I’m outside my body watching myself or anything like that. And the world doesn’t seem unreal to me. It’s more ordinary than that — like my attention drifts, not like I’m detached from myself.

So, no, I haven’t really noticed anything like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms that suggest a possible psychotic disorder, such as depersonalization or derealization, which could help differentiate between the remaining diagnostic candidates.
doctor.question: Have you ever had moments where you felt like your thoughts were not your own, or that someone else could hear or influence them?

target_item.reason: The question is about psychotic-like experiences such as thought insertion, thought broadcasting, or external influence over thoughts, which are not covered by the ADHD inattentive symptom profile provided.

patient.answer:
No, I can’t say I’ve ever had that. I mean, I’ve had plenty of times where my thoughts feel scattered or I’m not following my own train of thought very well, but they still feel like mine.

I’ve never felt like someone else put a thought in my head, or like my thoughts were being broadcast or heard by other people. And I don’t feel like anyone can control or influence them in that way. If I’m influenced by someone, it’s more the normal kind of thing, like somebody says something and then I think about it, not like they’re reaching into my mind or anything.

So no, I haven’t noticed anything like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant decline in cognitive function that could indicate F06.8 (Other specified mental disorders due to known physiological condition).
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant changes in your memory or thinking that have gotten worse over time, like forgetting important events or struggling with tasks that used to be easy for you?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: Lately I’ve forgotten things I meant to do, like returning a call from the doctor’s office, picking up a prescription, or leaving the house on time for one of my cousin’s appointments.
target_item.reason: The question is most directly asking about worsening memory/forgetfulness in day-to-day functioning, such as forgetting important tasks or appointments.

patient.answer:
I wouldn’t say it’s been some big, dramatic decline, like I’m forgetting major life events or suddenly can’t do things I used to know how to do. It’s more these everyday things that I meant to take care of, and then they just don’t happen unless something reminds me.

Like I mentioned, returning a call from the doctor’s office — I knew I needed to do it, and I even had that thought more than once, but somehow the day went by and I still hadn’t done it. Same with picking up a prescription. It wasn’t that I didn’t care or didn’t understand it was important; it just slipped out of my mind at the wrong time.

And leaving the house on time has been another one. There was one of my cousin’s appointments where I needed to be ready and out the door, and I thought I was managing the time okay, but then I realized I was behind and rushing. So it’s more that kind of forgetfulness or losing track of what I’m supposed to be doing next. It’s frustrating, but I don’t think of it as me forgetting big important events so much as missing these practical day-to-day things.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms primarily related to attention, focus, and memory issues without mood symptoms, to differentiate between F06.8 (Other specified mental disorders) and mood disorder candidates (F32.9, F33.9).
doctor.question: Can you describe how long you’ve been experiencing these difficulties with attention, focus, and forgetfulness, and whether you feel they are significantly affecting your ability to function in your daily life?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been noticeably harder for about 11 months, since my cousin moved in with us after surgery.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the attention, focus, and forgetfulness difficulties have been present; although they also ask about impairment, the duration portion is the most direct match.

patient.answer:
It’s been, I’d say, noticeably harder for about 11 months now. I can kind of place it because it lines up with when my cousin moved in with us after surgery. Before that, I’m not saying I was perfectly organized or anything, but it didn’t feel like it was getting in the way in the same way.

Since then, with more going on at home and more things to keep track of, I’ve noticed the attention and forgetfulness more. It’s not like I can’t function at all, but it does affect my day-to-day life. I’ll miss little but important things, or I’ll need more reminders, or I’ll lose track of time and then everything becomes rushed. So yes, it’s affecting me, just maybe not in a catastrophic way — more like a constant, frustrating interference.

inference.note: This turn ruled out F32.9 and F33.9 by confirming that the patient does not meet criteria for major depressive disorder (no persistent low mood, anhedonia, or functional impairment consistent with depression). The longitudinal course and cognitive symptoms are more consistent with F06.8 (mild neurocognitive disorder due to medical condition or medication, or unspecified), especially given the 11-month duration and functional impact of attentional and memory difficulties.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are better explained by a neurocognitive disorder or if ADHD is still the leading candidate.
doctor.question: Have you had similar difficulties with attention, focus, and forgetfulness going back to your childhood or adolescence, or do you feel these problems started more recently, in adulthood?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even back in grade school, before I was 12, teachers told my parents I was bright but always daydreaming, leaving homework in my desk, and needing reminders to finish classwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the attention, focus, and forgetfulness difficulties were present in childhood or adolescence versus starting only in adulthood, which directly matches onset prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
I think some of it does go way back, actually. It’s not like I would have described it the same way when I was a kid, of course, but looking back, there were signs.

Even in grade school, before I was 12, I remember teachers telling my parents things like, “He’s bright, but he’s always daydreaming,” or that I wasn’t finishing my work unless someone kept reminding me. I’d leave homework in my desk instead of bringing it home, or I’d do part of something and then sort of drift off and not complete the classwork. It wasn’t that I didn’t understand it — that was the frustrating part, I think, for teachers and probably my parents too. It was more like I just wasn’t staying with it.

So, the problems feel more noticeable recently as an adult, especially with more responsibilities, but when you ask whether there were similar patterns in childhood, yes, I think there were. They just weren’t framed the same way back then.

inference.note: The patient reported lifelong difficulties with attention and focus, dating back to childhood, with recent exacerbation due to increased responsibilities. This, combined with current symptoms of inattention, forgetfulness, and executive dysfunction without evidence of mood episodes, psychotic symptoms, or dissociation, points toward a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, predominantly inattentive presentation, based on a persistent pattern of inattention and forgetfulness that began in childhood, continues into adulthood, and causes functional impairment in daily life, especially under increased responsibility.
